references.text: This text expresses the same essential unity between Father and Son as in John 14:11, where Jesus says, 'I am in the Father and the Father is in me.' Here Jesus affirms: 'I and the Father are one,' which forms the theological basis for believing in him through his works.

Jesus links faith in him directly to faith in the Father, just as in John 14:11. He explains that whoever sees him has seen the Father, and that faith in him is faith in the one who sent him, underscoring the mutuality of their relationship.

Here the full dependence and unity between Son and Father are described: the Son can do nothing on his own, but only what he sees the Father doing. This is the same dynamic Jesus refers to when he urges the disciples to believe in him because of his works.

In this high-priestly prayer, Jesus asks that the disciples may be one, just as the Father and Son are one. This repeats the theme of inner unity central to John 14:11, which serves as proof that God has sent Jesus.

Just before verse 11, Jesus explains that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He asks Philip, 'Have I been with you so long, and yet you do not know me?' and confirms that the Father dwells in him and does his works through him, which is the direct context for believing in him because of his works.
